request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary

Patient Information:
Name: Anonymous
Gender: Female
Age: 25
Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient was administered with various medications including alprazolam 500 μg, duloxetine 90 mg, olanzapine 5 mg, haloperidol 2.5 mg, clonazepam, baclofen, diazepam, phenytoin, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, levodopa, oral baclofen, lacosamide and potassium channel antagonist 3,4 diaminopyridine.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with vomiting, bilateral leg pain, difficulty mobilising and flexed posture of her neck. She later developed visual and auditory hallucinations, respiratory failure with a coma scale score of 3, hypertensive, tachycardic, pyrexic and severe limb rigidity. Subsequently, contractures of the hands and feet were also developed. The patient was intubated and ventilated. The patient intermittently reported visual hallucinations throughout the hospital admission. Further complications included ileus, ischaemic bowel and sepsis.

Outcome:
The patient showed marked clinical improvement with the administration of potassium channel antagonist 3,4 diaminopyridine. This resulted in extubation, multiple medication decreases, transfer from ICU, and ultimately discharged home sixteen months after admission. The patient is now dependent on others for all activities of daily living and has developed contractures of the upper and lower limbs. There have been no documented seizures since discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient requires long-term follow-up care for contractures of the upper and lower limbs. The patient may also benefit from genetic counselling and additional investigations as advised by the neurology team.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
This presentation suggests a stiff-person spectrum disorder, specifically progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM), or possibly an antibody-mediated variant such as glycine receptor antibodies. The features are limb rigidity, flexed neck, hallucinations, respiratory failure, autonomic instability, and a response to 3,4-diaminopyridine. Treatments such as baclofen and benzodiazepines also fit this picture.

The alternative is hyperekplexia or a channelopathy. The follow-up mention of genetic counselling points toward a genetic cause, and the response to a potassium channel blocker suggests a potassium channel disorder. A KCNA1 or similar variant could produce episodic ataxia or neuromyotonia, but the case reads more like a gain-of-function potassium channel encephalopathy, such as a KCNC1 or KCNMA1 variant. These are epileptic or movement disorders and would still be coded in G.

Stiff-person syndrome is coded G25.8 in ICD-10 (G25.8 other specified extrapyramidal and movement disorders). In ICD-10-AM, stiff-man syndrome is also G25.8. Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity could be G04.8 or G37. Isaacs syndrome (neuromyotonia) is G71.1 in ICD-10 and is classed under myotonic disorders.

The picture here includes severe rigidity, hallucinations, autonomic instability and contractures. Neuromyotonia (Isaacs) with encephalopathy would be Morvan syndrome, which is coded G71.1 (myotonic disorders). Morvan syndrome features neuromyotonia, hallucinations, autonomic instability and insomnia, and 3,4-diaminopyridine is a typical treatment. The chapter G block that includes it is G70–G73, so the category is G71.

Given the options, though, the stiff-person spectrum (G25) is the other candidate. Morvan syndrome with CASPR2 antibodies fits better with the hallucinations, autonomic features, and a response to a potassium channel blocker. However, the genetic counselling comment and the sixteen-month course suggest a genetic channelopathy, which would still be a G category.

I'll go with G71.

CODE: G71
